result:
There is a strange, persistent illusion that time speeds up as we get older, sliding through our fingers like dry sand while we remain helplessly stationary. Children spend entire epochs waiting for summer vacation, each Tuesday stretching out like a vast, undiscovered continent. But somewhere around our twenties, the calendar shifts gears. Months blur into quarters, years telescope into decades, and suddenly we are wondering how a decade evaporated between the release of a movie and its anniversary. 

Yet, I am not entirely convinced time is accelerating. I suspect, rather, that our brains simply stop recording the mundane. When you are seven years old, everything is startlingly novel. The texture of tree bark, the specific smell of rain on hot asphalt, the intricate politics of the playground—these are high-definition experiences, heavy with data. As adults, we build cognitive shortcuts. We commute the same route, drink the same coffee from the same mug, process the same types of emails, and categorize these events as “the daily grind.” Because our brains are no longer expending energy to map familiar territory, the memories fail to stick. We live on autopilot, and an unrecorded life feels as though it never truly happened.

This realization is both terrifying and liberating. It suggests that the antidote to the disappearing years is not trying to slow down the clock—an impossible mechanical endeavor—but rather violently disrupting our own complacency. It means staring at the bark on the tree again. It means taking the unfamiliar side street just to see where it leads, even if it adds ten minutes to the trip. 

Consider, for a moment, the sheer improbability of existence. We are perched on a damp, spinning rock hurtling through a cold, indifferent vacuum at roughly sixty-seven thousand miles per hour. Around us, ancient stars collapse into black holes, nebulas bloom in violent clouds of gas and dust, and the universe expands inexorably into the dark. And yet, here we are, drinking fermented bean juice and worrying about whether we replied to a work message with the correct degree of professional enthusiasm. 

We spend so much of our brief, incandescent window of consciousness worrying about the wrong things. We rehearse embarrassing moments from ten years ago in the shower. We construct elaborate mental fortresses to protect our egos from slights that no one else even remembers. We defer joy, promising ourselves that we will finally relax, travel, write that book, or learn that instrument *once things settle down*. 

Spoiler alert: things never settle down. Chaos is the natural state of the universe. Order is merely a temporary, localized ceasefire that we carve out with immense effort. 

If you wait for the perfect conditions to start living your actual life, you will wait forever. There will always be a bill to pay, a laundry basket overflowing, a geopolitical crisis on the news, a nagging ache in your lower back. Waiting for permission from the universe to be happy is like waiting for a traffic light that will never turn green because you are parked in a grocery store parking lot. 

This brings me to the beauty of purposelessness. In our hyper-capitalist, efficiency-obsessed culture, every hobby must be monetized, every walk must be tracked on a smartwatch to ensure an optimal heart-rate zone, and every book read must be logged to fulfill an annual challenge. We have turned leisure into another job. 

What happens if we drop the scorecard? What if we do something purely because it is ridiculous, inefficient, and entirely useless? 

Go paint a terrible watercolor of a potato. Sit on a park bench and watch pigeons fight over a crust of bread for an hour without pulling out your phone to check your notifications. Write a terrible poem about the sound of a refrigerator humming in an empty kitchen. Allow yourself the profound dignity of being bad at something simply because you enjoy the sensation of doing it. 

We are so terrified of failure that we often refuse to play the game at all unless we are guaranteed victory. But mastery is overrated. Mastery is cold, clinical, and finished. The magic lives entirely in the fumbling, awkward beginning—the moment of pure potential where you do not know what you are doing, and the canvas is still entirely open.

Think about the objects we surround ourselves with, too. We live in an era of seamless glass and polished aluminum, where everything is designed to be sleek, disposable, and frictionless. But friction is where character is born. Think of an old wooden table with deep gouges in the surface from decades of family dinners, or a paperback book with a cracked spine, dog-eared pages, and notes scrawled in the margins. These objects bear the scars of a lived-in reality. They tell a story. 

When we smooth away all the rough edges of our lives in the pursuit of perfection, we also sand away the grip points. We make it impossible for anything to hold onto us, and for us to hold onto anything. 

Perhaps that is why we find such deep comfort in nature, despite our best efforts to pave over it. A forest does not care about your productivity metrics. A mountain does not validate your LinkedIn profile. The ocean does not care if you have inbox zero. When you stand at the edge of the sea, watching waves crash against ancient stones that have been worn smooth over millennia, your anxieties do not necessarily vanish, but they are put into their proper proportion. You realize that you are not the main character of the universe; you are merely a transient guest, lucky enough to witness the show for a few fleeting decades.

And what a magnificent show it is, if we only bother to look up from our glowing rectangles. 

Think of the sheer sensory overload of being human. We have evolved receptors that translate microscopic vibrations in the air into the soaring melodies of a symphony. We have photoreceptors that allow us to perceive the impossible, burning oranges and purples of a sunset. We have the capacity for language—the bizarre, borderline magical trick of pressing air past our vocal cords in specific patterns to transfer complex emotional landscapes directly into the mind of another person. 

We can share the grief of a poet who died three hundred years ago, or feel the anticipatory thrill of an author who hasn't been born yet. We can taste salt and sugar, feel the electric shock of cold water on a summer afternoon, and hold the hand of someone we love while the world burns down around us.

We are walking miracles, wrapped in fragile packages of skin and bone, staggering through the dark with matches in our pockets. 

So strike a match. Burn brightly. Be loud and messy and unapologetically curious. Do not save your best china for a special occasion, because the special occasion is right now, in this messy, chaotic, unrepeatable second. Eat the cake first. Say the thing you are afraid to say. Forgive yourself for the mistakes you made yesterday, because the version of you that made them is already gone, replaced by someone new, someone who is still figuring it all out.

We are all just winging it, every single one of us, from the toddlers on the playground to the CEOs in corner offices and the philosophers in their towers. Nobody has a map of this territory because the map is being drawn as we walk. 

So take a step off the beaten path. Look up at the stars. Feel the cold air in your lungs, the beating of your heart, the undeniable, stubborn fact that you are here, right now, against all mathematical odds. 

That is enough. It has always been enough.
